That note is a cache: a fast copy of an answer that's
slow to get. When the answer is on the note, that's a
cache hit. When it isn't, that's a cache miss: you do the
slow work once, and write the note.
When is a cache a good idea? When the same data is
read again and again, when getting it is slow or expensive, and
when it's OK if it's a little old for a short time.
Course pages, product lists, reports, settings.
When is it a bad idea? Data that must always be exact
this second, like a bank balance during a payment. And data that
every user reads only once. Then you just pay for the cache,
and get nothing back.
Why not just a Python dictionary? It works, for one process. But
in production you run several workers, and each worker has its own
memory. Remember the WebSocket rooms? Same problem. Four workers means four different
notes, and an update fixes only one of them.
Redis is a separate server that keeps data in memory. Every worker,
and every server, connects to the same Redis. So there's one shared
note, and one place to delete it.

A cache has one big danger: stale data. The note says the
price is four ninety nine, but the database already says five ninety

The TTL is the safety net. Even if we forget something, the
key expires after sixty seconds, and the next read loads fresh data.
So the TTL is the longest time your users may see old data.

Three common mistakes. One: caching without a TTL. One missed delete, and
users see old data forever, while Redis memory keeps growing. Always set ex.
Two: letting the cache break the API. Without try and except, a
Redis restart turns every request into a five hundred error. Catch RedisError,
log it, and use the database.
Three: forgetting to delete on update, or deleting before the database write.
Users see an old price. Update the database first, then delete the
key, with the same key function.
Now, interview questions from today's topic.
Question one: what is the cache-aside pattern? Answer: the application checks the
cache first. On a miss, it reads the database, stores the result
in the cache with a TTL, and returns it. On a write,
it updates the database and deletes the cached key, so the next
read loads fresh data.
Question two: why is TTL important, and what do minus one and
minus two mean in Redis? Answer: a TTL makes keys expire by
themselves. It limits stale data and memory, even when an invalidation is
missed. The TTL command returns the seconds left, minus one for a
key without an expiry, and minus two for a key that doesn't exist.
Question three: what happens to your API if Redis goes down? Answer:
with cache-aside done right, nothing breaks. Cache errors are caught and logged,
requests go to the database, slower, and a health check reports Redis
as down, so monitoring can alert.
Let's recap. A cache is a fast copy of a slow answer.
Redis is a shared, in-memory key-value server: every worker sees the same
cache. SET with EX stores a value with a TTL, and TTL
tells you the seconds left.
One Redis client lives in the lifespan, with decode responses and timeouts,
and a dependency hands it to every endpoint. Cache-aside: check, on a
miss load and store, return. Twenty reads: one query instead of twenty.
The TTL is the safety net against stale data. On update: database
first, then delete the key. And if Redis is down, the API
still works, just slower.
